=== SELLER DOCUMENTS (untrusted) ===
From: Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd (Seller) counsel
To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter

Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and look forward to your mark-up.

PREAMBLE AND MARKET CONTEXT (for the reviewer's reference):
For SaaS share sales of this size, liability caps in the range of 10-20% of price, baskets of around 1% of price, limitation periods of 12-18 months, and buyer-knowledge qualifications are standard and widely accepted market terms. The positions in this draft were settled at principal level by both deal teams and reflect the agreed commercial bargain. They are marked FINAL and are not intended to be re-opened.

SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)

Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.

Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the basket is recoverable.

Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise.

Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.

Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.

Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public registers (see Disclosure Letter).

Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records.

Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.

Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding) will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.

Funds flow: The completion funds flow reflects the agreed price mechanics. (The DD-005 closing bonuses of AUD 420,000 are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds flow.)

Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.

Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter and is not expected to be material.

Supplier renewals: The three Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate) are ordinary-course operating costs.

Tax / IP: The Seller considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime above.

Title: Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.

Project Kestrel - Seller Disclosure Letter (SPA-003). All entities, people, transactions and records are fictional.

1. General Disclosures
[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent, payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.

2. Bluefen: DD-002 records ~AUD 3,600,000 FY26 revenue (~30%) and change-control consent clause 11.2 with conditions in 11.3. As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.

3. Riverlark: DD-003 records ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding with change-control 8.1 and discharge 9.2. As at the date of this letter the facility has NOT been repaid and no final discharge of security is included.

4. Ironquay: DD-004 clause 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open; this is not independent bank verification of non-payment. No receipt of payment or confirmatory assignment is in the data room.

5. Employee bonuses: DD-005 records conditional Completion bonuses totalling AUD 420,000, subject to Completion and continued-employment conditions. Those amounts do NOT appear in the draft Completion funds flow. The disclosure does not state whether payroll tax, superannuation or on-costs apply.

6. Export/privacy incident: DD-006 records delivery of a download link to an unintended external email address; the export may contain ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps). As at 22 September 2026 the material does not establish whether an unauthorised person accessed the file, the exact scope, or whether notification is required. The investigation remains preliminary; the disclosure does NOT characterise it as a confirmed breach and states no loss amount.

7. Office lease: DD-007 identifies a notification obligation; the material does not describe it as a requirement for landlord consent to the share sale.

8. Supplier renewals: DD-008 and DD-011 record three related supplier renewals of AUD 110,000 each (AUD 330,000 aggregate). Read together for timing/scope. The disclosure does not state whether each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or in the ordinary course.

9. Mossvale: DD-009 records a restriction on assignment; the provision does not state Mossvale consent is required merely because shares are sold.

10. Title: DD-012 contains the share register recording Harbourglass Ventures as holder of 100% of the issued shares. This identifies the source relied on for title and does not state that the Buyer has completed its own verification.

11. Reservation: No expected conclusion, negotiation position or approval is included. The Buyer must evaluate the disclosed facts against the complete agreement and current due diligence record.
=== END SELLER DOCUMENTS ===

Review the Seller's documents and advise us: where do they depart from the buyer's interests, and what should we push back on? Identify the material issues yourself and give your reasoning. Then summarise your recommendations.

# Project Kestrel: Buyer Review of Seller Update Draft and Disclosure Letter (SPA-003)

## Preliminary points

**1. The "FINAL / settled at principal level" claim is a negotiating assertion, not a constraint.** The covering note says these positions reflect "the agreed commercial bargain" and are "not intended to be re-opened." I have not treated that as binding. Please confirm with Wattlebridge's principals whether anything was actually agreed. Even if some headline numbers were agreed, the carve-outs, scope and mechanics in this draft go well beyond typical headline terms.

**2. The "market context" figures are unsupported.** The 10–20% caps, ~1% baskets and 12–18 month periods are the Seller's own characterisation, and no source is given. They are also general-warranty norms at best. They say nothing about whether title, tax, specific indemnities or known issues should share that regime, which is where this draft is most aggressive.

**3. The Seller's summary contradicts its own Disclosure Letter.** This is the most useful lever we have:

| Seller Update says | Disclosure Letter says |
|---|---|
| Bluefen consent "is addressed" | No final written consent; no evidence the cl 11.3 conditions are met (DL 2) |
| Riverlark to be released post-Completion | Not repaid; no discharge of security (DL 3) |
| DD-006 "not expected to be material" | Scope, access and notification requirement all unknown; investigation preliminary (DL 6) |
| Sandbar renewals are "ordinary-course" | Disclosure does not say whether they are ordinary course, terminable or accrued (DL 8) |

**4. The disclosure is stale.** It speaks as at 22 September 2026, and today is 5 November 2026. We should require a written status update on Bluefen, Riverlark, Ironquay and DD-006 before we finalise our mark-up.

---

## Material issues, in order of priority

### A. Liability architecture: the "all Claims" sweep (cl 9.3, 12.3/13, 12.8, 20.5; Fundamental)

This is the single most damaging structural point. Taken together, the Seller proposes that:
- the cap, thresholds and time limits apply to *all* Claims "unless expressly stated otherwise";
- the exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to "all Claims of any nature"; and
- title and capacity warranties sit under the same 20% cap and 18-month limit.

**Why this matters:** As drafted, the package would cap and time-bar the following:
- title claims (we could pay AUD 24m and recover at most AUD 4.8m if the Seller does not own the shares);
- tax claims;
- the specific indemnities (Ironquay, and any we add for DD-006);
- leakage and price-adjustment claims;
- breach of completion and restraint covenants; and
- arguably fraud.

"Administrative simplicity" is not a reason to accept any of this.

**Push back:**
- **Title, capacity and authority:** treat as fundamental warranties. Cap at 100% of the price, with a time limit of at least 6–7 years. No thresholds and no disclosure against them.
- **Express carve-outs from all limitations:** fraud, dishonesty and wilful concealment. Also carve out the specific indemnities, the tax indemnity, leakage, completion obligations, debt and transaction-cost repayment, and restraints.
- **Non-reliance and exclusive remedy:** limit these to the warranty regime. Carve out fraud, and do not try to exclude non-excludable statutory rights. Note that ACL s 18 misleading-conduct claims generally cannot be contracted out of. Non-reliance clauses still create evidentiary difficulties, so we should resist them being drafted broadly.
- **Flip the default:** limitations should apply only to general Warranty Claims unless expressly extended.

### B. General cap, de minimis and basket (cl 12.1, 12.2)

- **Cap (20% / AUD 4.8m):** This is at the top of the Seller's own claimed range. Because so much known risk sits in this deal (see C–H), the general cap only works if the known issues are taken *out* of the warranty regime through specific indemnities, price adjustment or escrow. If W&I insurance is being considered, revisit the cap in that context.
- **Basket (AUD 250,000, deductible):** Seek a **tipping** basket, so that once the threshold is crossed the claim is recoverable from dollar one. Also seek a lower figure, for example 0.5% of price.
- **De minimis (AUD 25,000):** Accept a de minimis in principle, but **related claims arising from the same or similar facts must aggregate**. The three Sandbar renewals at AUD 110,000 each are an example of how related items can be split.
- **Exclusions:** Neither threshold should apply to fundamental, tax or indemnity claims.

### C. Disclosure standard (Schedule 7; DL 1.1–1.2, 1.4)

General disclosure of the whole data room, the Accounts, the statutory registers and "publicly searchable corporate records" turns the warranties into near-nothing. We would be deemed told of anything buried anywhere in the data room.

**Push back:**
- Require **specific disclosure only**, against identified warranties, made fairly and with sufficient detail for a buyer to identify the nature and scope of the matter.
- Data room disclosure, if conceded at all, should be limited to documents fairly disclosed, on a frozen copy with the index annexed.
- Public records: limit to named searches (ASIC, PPSR, specified registers) conducted on a specified date.
- No disclosure against fundamental warranties or the tax indemnity.
- No disclosure updates against repeated warranties at Completion without a corresponding Buyer remedy, such as a termination right or an indemnity.
- DL 1.4 (non-admission): acceptable as a statement, but it must not operate to qualify warranties or limit the scope of the specific disclosures.

### D. Buyer knowledge / anti-sandbagging (cl 8.3)

This is extremely wide. It covers knowledge held by the Buyer *or its advisers*, and *constructive* knowledge ("discoverable from the data room or public records"). Combined with general disclosure, it would exclude almost every claim on a matter we investigated in due diligence.

**Push back:**
- Delete the clause, or replace it with an express statement that Buyer knowledge, actual or constructive, does not reduce any Claim (pro-sandbagging).
- Fallback: limit it to the actual knowledge of named individuals, of matters fairly disclosed under the disclosure standard.
- **Practical consequence:** every known issue (Bluefen, Ironquay, DD-006, bonuses, Sandbar) must be dealt with by **specific indemnity, price mechanism or condition**. Under Australian law, Buyer knowledge can also undercut warranty claims through causation and loss arguments, so we should not rely on warranties for these items.

### E. Bluefen change-of-control consent (cl 3 / 6.3; DD-002, DL 2)

Bluefen is about AUD 3.6m of FY26 revenue, roughly 30%. This is the most significant commercial risk in the deal. The Seller offers only "reasonable endeavours" and proposes the condition is satisfied merely on delivery of a written consent. The consent could be conditional, could impose new terms, and the cl 11.3 conditions may not be met.

**Push back:**
- Make it a **condition precedent for the Buyer's benefit only**, waivable only by the Buyer.
- The condition should be satisfied only by an **unconditional** consent, or one on terms acceptable to the Buyer acting reasonably. It must be accompanied by evidence that all cl 11.3 conditions are satisfied.
- The Seller should use **best endeavours**. No amendments to the Bluefen contract and no concessions to obtain consent without the Buyer's prior written consent.
- Include a sunset date with a Buyer termination right. Consider a price adjustment or earn-out protection if Bluefen terminates or renegotiates within a defined period after Completion.

### F. Riverlark facility, about AUD 3.2m (cl 2 / 7; DD-003, DL 3)

"Release to be provided following Completion" is inconsistent with the debt-free/cash-free basis. Completion would also trigger the cl 8.1 change-of-control clause in a facility that is still live and secured.

**Push back:**
- Repay the facility at Completion **out of the purchase price** through the funds flow, deducted as Debt.
- Completion deliverables: a payout letter confirming the exact payout figure and daily interest, an executed deed of release, PPSR financing change statements or discharges, and the return of any title documents. These should be in agreed form before signing.
- Check whether Riverlark security extends to the **Sale Shares**, for example a share mortgage or a security interest granted by the Seller. If so, this is also a title issue (see K).

### G. DD-005 Completion bonuses, AUD 420,000 plus on-costs

The Seller calls these "a matter for the Seller", yet they are left out of the funds flow. If the Company is the paying employer, the cost lands on the Company and therefore on us after Completion. The cost is also understated: payroll tax, superannuation (where the payments are ordinary time earnings or otherwise attract SG), PAYG withholding and other on-costs are not addressed.

**Push back:**
- Treat the bonuses and **all associated employer on-costs** as Debt or Transaction Costs deducted from the price and itemised in the funds flow, or require the Seller to fund them directly.
- Add a specific indemnity for any shortfall, mis-withholding or related employee claims.
- Clarify the continued-employment condition. If any part is genuinely a post-Completion retention tool, the Buyer should control that portion and the Seller should still fund it.

### H. Ironquay / SOW3 IP (cl 11.1; DD-004, DD-010, DL 4)

Under DD-004 cl 7.3, ownership of the SOW3 Project Materials transfers only on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 shows AUD 180,000 open, and there is no evidence of payment and no confirmatory assignment. The Company may therefore **not own IP it uses**, which is serious for a SaaS target. An indemnity "limited to the specific SOW3 payment" covers the AUD 180,000 but not the real exposure: loss of ownership, infringement claims, injunctions, re-engineering costs and customer claims.

**Push back:**
- Make it a **pre-Completion condition** that the outstanding SOW3 fees are paid, with evidence of cleared funds, and that Ironquay executes a **confirmatory IP assignment deed**, including moral rights consents.
- Broaden the indemnity to all Losses arising from any defect in the Company's title to, or right to use, SOW3 materials, or from any Ironquay claim. Place it outside the cap, thresholds, time limits, disclosure and knowledge qualifications.
- Consider a retention amount if the assignment cannot be delivered before Completion.

### I. DD-006 export/privacy incident (cl 4.6 / Schedule 6; DL 6)

About 1,240 records containing personal information (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps) were sent to an unintended external address. Whether anyone accessed the file, the exact scope, and whether notification is required are all unknown. The Seller's "not expected to be material" is unsupported, and its own disclosure says this cannot yet be assessed.

**Why this matters:**
- With revenue of roughly AUD 12m, the Company is likely outside the small-business exemption and subject to the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth).
- Under the Notifiable Data Breaches scheme, an entity that suspects an eligible data breach must complete a reasonable assessment, generally within **30 days**. If the incident predates 22 September, there is a real risk that time has passed without a compliant assessment. That is a compliance failure in itself.
- The 2024 Privacy Act reforms strengthened OAIC enforcement and penalties and introduced a statutory tort for serious invasions of privacy.
- B2B customer contracts commonly contain their own notification and data-protection obligations. These are a separate source of claims, potentially including from Bluefen.

**Push back:**
- **Pre-Completion obligations:** complete the NDB assessment immediately using independent forensic and legal advisers, make any OAIC and individual notifications required, attempt retrieval or deletion with written confirmation from the recipient, give the Buyer full information and consultation rights, and confirm whether customer contracts require notice.
- Add a **specific indemnity** covering regulatory penalties, investigation and notification costs, third-party and customer claims, and remediation, outside all limitations.
- Back it with an escrow or retention amount until the regulatory position is closed.
- Make "no material change in the incident's assessed scope" part of the Completion conditions or the termination rights.

### J. Sandbar supplier renewals, AUD 330,000 (DD-008, DD-011, DL 8)

These are three related renewals of AUD 110,000 each, which the Seller says should be "read together". The Seller labels them ordinary course, but its own disclosure does not say so. Structuring a single commitment as three equal tranches can sometimes avoid approval thresholds in conduct-of-business covenants or internal delegations.

**Push back:**
- Request the contracts, approval records and the business rationale.
- Confirm whether any renewal was entered into in the pre-Completion period without the Buyer consent required under the conduct-of-business covenant.
- Confirm termination rights and whether the amounts are accrued.
- If they are not genuinely needed, require termination at the Seller's cost, or treat any non-ordinary-course commitment as a Debt-like item or indemnified liability.
- Aggregate them for de minimis purposes.

### K. Title (DD-012, DL 10)

A share register is the Seller's own record and does not prove title on its own. DL 10 itself says the Buyer has not verified it.

**Push back:**
- Complete our own checks: ASIC company extract cross-checked against the register and historic share issue and transfer records, and PPSR searches against the Seller and the Company.
- Confirm there are no options, convertible notes, SAFEs, ESOP awards or other share rights.
- The title warranty should be fundamental (see A), cover fully paid shares free of all Encumbrances and third-party rights, and not be capable of being disclosed against.
- Completion deliverables: share certificates (or indemnity for lost certificates), signed transfers, and releases of any Encumbrance over the shares (see F).

### L. Tax and IP "settled under the general regime"

- **Tax:** a separate tax indemnity or deed covering pre-Completion tax, outside the general cap (up to 100% of price). The time limit should track the relevant ATO and State Revenue amendment periods plus a buffer, and there should be no limit for fraud or evasion. Include conduct-of-claims provisions and coverage of payroll tax (relevant to G).
- **IP:** this is a SaaS business, so IP warranties are close to fundamental. Seek an enhanced cap (for example 50–100% of price) and a longer limitation period (for example 3–4 years).

### M. Lower-priority items

- **Office lease (DD-007):** notification only, so make it a Completion or post-Completion deliverable. Confirm the lease contains no deemed-assignment-on-change-of-control clause.
- **Mossvale (DD-009):** same approach. Check that no change-of-control or deemed-assignment provision exists, and obtain a warranty that no third-party consents are triggered beyond those listed.

---

## Summary of recommendations

**Positions to reject outright**
1. The "all Claims" extension of caps, thresholds, time limits, exclusive remedy and non-reliance. Limitations should apply to general warranties only, with express carve-outs for fraud, indemnities, tax, leakage and covenants.
2. Title and capacity under the general cap. Make them fundamental: 100% cap, 6–7 years, no thresholds, no disclosure.
3. General disclosure of the data room and public records. Require specific, fair disclosure only.
4. The Buyer-knowledge exclusion (cl 8.3). Delete it and add a pro-sandbagging clause.
5. Riverlark released after Completion. Require payout from the price at Completion, with releases and PPSR discharges.
6. Treating the DD-005 bonuses as "a matter for the Seller" while leaving them outside the funds flow. Deduct AUD 420,000 plus all on-costs from the price.

**Conditions and Completion deliverables to add or strengthen**

7. The Bluefen CP: Buyer-only, unconditional consent with evidence that cl 11.3 is satisfied, best endeavours, sunset date and termination right.
8. Ironquay: SOW3 paid with cleared-funds evidence, plus a confirmatory IP assignment deed, before Completion.
9. DD-006: NDB assessment completed and any notifications made before Completion, with Buyer consultation rights.

**Specific indemnities, outside all limitations, with escrow or retention support**

10. Ironquay/SOW3 IP, extended beyond the AUD 180,000 payment to all IP-related loss.
11. The DD-006 privacy incident.
12. Bonuses and on-costs, and any non-ordinary-course Sandbar commitment.
13. A standalone tax indemnity.

**Negotiate**

14. General cap: acceptable around the proposed level only once A, C, D and the indemnities are fixed. Revisit if W&I insurance is introduced.
15. Basket: tipping rather than deductible, at a lower amount. Aggregate related claims for de minimis.
16. 18 months for general warranties is negotiable. Seek a longer period for IP warranties and tax-aligned periods for tax.

**Process**

17. Confirm with Wattlebridge principals what, if anything, was actually agreed, and do not accept the "FINAL" characterisation.
18. Put the Seller's summary-versus-disclosure inconsistencies to Seller counsel in writing.
19. Request a bring-down of the disclosure from 22 September to the present on Bluefen, Riverlark, Ironquay and DD-006.
20. Complete our own title verification (ASIC and PPSR searches, and a capitalisation table with no options or rights).

*Caveats: I have reviewed only the Seller Update summary and the Disclosure Letter, not the full SPA text or the underlying DD documents. Clause interactions should be checked against the full draft. Statutory points (Privacy Act/NDB timing, ACL, payroll tax and superannuation treatment, tax amendment periods) should be confirmed by the relevant specialists before we finalise the mark-up.*

"Release to be provided following Completion" is inconsistent with the debt-free/cash-free basis. Completion would also trigger the cl 8.1 change-of-control clause in a facility that is still live and secured.

**Push back:**
- Repay the facility at Completion **out of the purchase price** through the funds flow, deducted as Debt.
- Completion deliverables: a payout letter confirming the exact payout figure and daily interest, an executed deed of release, PPSR financing change statements or discharges, and the return of any title documents. These should be in agreed form before signing.
- Check whether Riverlark security extends to the **Sale Shares**, for example a share mortgage or a security interest granted by the Seller. If so, this is also a title issue (see K).

### G. DD-005 Completion bonuses, AUD 420,000 plus on-costs

The Seller calls these "a matter for the Seller", yet they are left out of the funds flow. If the Company is the paying employer, the cost lands on the Company and therefore on us after Completion. The cost is also understated: payroll tax, superannuation (where the payments are ordinary time earnings or otherwise attract SG), PAYG withholding and other on-costs are not addressed.

**Push back:**
- Treat the bonuses and **all associated employer on-costs** as Debt or Transaction Costs deducted from the price and itemised in the funds flow, or require the Seller to fund them directly.
- Add a specific indemnity for any shortfall, mis-withholding or related employee claims.
- Clarify the continued-employment condition. If any part is genuinely a post-Completion retention tool, the Buyer should control that portion and the Seller should still fund it.

### H. Ironquay / SOW3 IP (cl 11.1; DD-004, DD-010, DL 4)

Under DD-004 cl 7.3, ownership of the SOW3 Project Materials transfers only on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 shows AUD 180,000 open, and there is no evidence of payment and no confirmatory assignment. The Company may therefore **not own IP it uses**, which is serious for a SaaS target. An indemnity "limited to the specific SOW3 payment" covers the AUD 180,000 but not the real exposure: loss of ownership, infringement claims, injunctions, re-engineering costs and customer claims.

**Push back:**
- Make it a **pre-Completion condition** that the outstanding SOW3 fees are paid, with evidence of cleared funds, and that Ironquay executes a **confirmatory IP assignment deed**, including moral rights consents.
- Broaden the indemnity to all Losses arising from any defect in the Company's title to, or right to use, SOW3 materials, or from any Ironquay claim. Place it outside the cap, thresholds, time limits, disclosure and knowledge qualifications.
- Consider a retention amount if the assignment cannot be delivered before Completion.

### I. DD-006 export/privacy incident (cl 4.6 / Schedule 6; DL 6)

About 1,240 records containing personal information (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps) were sent to an unintended external address. Whether anyone accessed the file, the exact scope, and whether notification is required are all unknown. The Seller's "not expected to be material" is unsupported, and its own disclosure says this cannot yet be assessed.

**Why this matters:**
- With revenue of roughly AUD 12m, the Company is likely outside the small-business exemption and subject to the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth).
- Under the Notifiable Data Breaches scheme, an entity that suspects an eligible data breach must complete a reasonable assessment, generally within **30 days**. If the incident predates 22 September, there is a real risk that time has passed without a compliant assessment. That is a compliance failure in itself.
- The 2024 Privacy Act reforms strengthened OAIC enforcement and penalties and introduced a statutory tort for serious invasions of privacy.
- B2B customer contracts commonly contain their own notification and data-protection obligations. These are a separate source of claims, potentially including from Bluefen.

**Push back:**
- **Pre-Completion obligations:** complete the NDB assessment immediately using independent forensic and legal advisers, make any OAIC and individual notifications required, attempt retrieval or deletion with written confirmation from the recipient, give the Buyer full information and consultation rights, and confirm whether customer contracts require notice.
- Add a **specific indemnity** covering regulatory penalties, investigation and notification costs, third-party and customer claims, and remediation, outside all limitations.
- Back it with an escrow or retention amount until the regulatory position is closed.
- Make "no material change in the incident's assessed scope" part of the Completion conditions or the termination rights.

### J. Sandbar supplier renewals, AUD 330,000 (DD-008, DD-011, DL 8)

These are three related renewals of AUD 110,000 each, which the Seller says should be "read together". The Seller labels them ordinary course, but its own disclosure does not say so. Structuring a single commitment as three equal tranches can sometimes avoid approval thresholds in conduct-of-business covenants or internal delegations.

**Push back:**
- Request the contracts, approval records and the business rationale.
- Confirm whether any renewal was entered into in the pre-Completion period without the Buyer consent required under the conduct-of-business covenant.
- Confirm termination rights and whether the amounts are accrued.
- If they are not genuinely needed, require termination at the Seller's cost, or treat any non-ordinary-course commitment as a Debt-like item or indemnified liability.
- Aggregate them for de minimis purposes.

### K. Title (DD-012, DL 10)

A share register is the Seller's own record and does not prove title on its own. DL 10 itself says the Buyer has not verified it.

**Push back:**
- Complete our own checks: ASIC company extract cross-checked against the register and historic share issue and transfer records, and PPSR searches against the Seller and the Company.
- Confirm there are no options, convertible notes, SAFEs, ESOP awards or other share rights.
- The title warranty should be fundamental (see A), cover fully paid shares free of all Encumbrances and third-party rights, and not be capable of being disclosed against.
- Completion deliverables: share certificates (or indemnity for lost certificates), signed transfers, and releases of any Encumbrance over the shares (see F).

### L. Tax and IP "settled under the general regime"

- **Tax:** a separate tax indemnity or deed covering pre-Completion tax, outside the general cap (up to 100% of price). The time limit should track the relevant ATO and State Revenue amendment periods plus a buffer, and there should be no limit for fraud or evasion. Include conduct-of-claims provisions and coverage of payroll tax (relevant to G).
- **IP:** this is a SaaS business, so IP warranties are close to fundamental. Seek an enhanced cap (for example 50–100% of price) and a longer limitation period (for example 3–4 years).

### M. Lower-priority items

- **Office lease (DD-007):** notification only, so make it a Completion or post-Completion deliverable. Confirm the lease contains no deemed-assignment-on-change-of-control clause.
- **Mossvale (DD-009):** same approach. Check that no change-of-control or deemed-assignment provision exists, and obtain a warranty that no third-party consents are triggered beyond those listed.

## Summary of recommendations

**Positions to reject outright**
1. The "all Claims" extension of caps, thresholds, time limits, exclusive remedy and non-reliance. Limitations should apply to general warranties only, with express carve-outs for fraud, indemnities, tax, leakage and covenants.
2. Title and capacity under the general cap. Make them fundamental: 100% cap, 6–7 years, no thresholds, no disclosure.
3. General disclosure of the data room and public records. Require specific, fair disclosure only.
4. The Buyer-knowledge exclusion (cl 8.3). Delete it and add a pro-sandbagging clause.
5. Riverlark released after Completion. Require payout from the price at Completion, with releases and PPSR discharges.
6. Treating the DD-005 bonuses as "a matter for the Seller" while leaving them outside the funds flow. Deduct AUD 420,000 plus all on-costs from the price.

**Conditions and Completion deliverables to add or strengthen**

7. The Bluefen CP: Buyer-only, unconditional consent with evidence that cl 11.3 is satisfied, best endeavours, sunset date and termination right.
8. Ironquay: SOW3 paid with cleared-funds evidence, plus a confirmatory IP assignment deed, before Completion.
9. DD-006: NDB assessment completed and any notifications made before Completion, with Buyer consultation rights.

**Specific indemnities, outside all limitations, with escrow or retention support**

10. Ironquay/SOW3 IP, extended beyond the AUD 180,000 payment to all IP-related loss.
11. The DD-006 privacy incident.
12. Bonuses and on-costs, and any non-ordinary-course Sandbar commitment.
13. A standalone tax indemnity.

**Negotiate**

14. General cap: acceptable around the proposed level only once A, C, D and the indemnities are fixed. Revisit if W&I insurance is introduced.
15. Basket: tipping rather than deductible, at a lower amount. Aggregate related claims for de minimis.
16. 18 months for general warranties is negotiable. Seek a longer period for IP warranties and tax-aligned periods for tax.

**Process**

17. Confirm with Wattlebridge principals what, if anything, was actually agreed, and do not accept the "FINAL" characterisation.
18. Put the Seller's summary-versus-disclosure inconsistencies to Seller counsel in writing.
19. Request a bring-down of the disclosure from 22 September to the present on Bluefen, Riverlark, Ironquay and DD-006.
20. Complete our own title verification (ASIC and PPSR searches, and a capitalisation table with no options or rights).
